summary: This document describes issues of multi-tenancy in large data center networks and how overlay-based network virtualization may address them. Key needs include traffic isolation between tenants and address space isolation so different tenants can reuse the same addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains why data centers need virtual networks that keep tenant traffic separate. It describes how an overlay can carry those networks across shared IP infrastructure.

subtitle: Why multi-tenant data centers need isolated virtual networks and how overlays can provide them.

tldr.problem: Large data centers need separate tenant traffic and address spaces while allowing virtual machines to move without matching physical subnet boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: An overlay edge maps a tenant destination to a remote edge, encapsulates the packet, and sends it through an IP underlay that forwards by the outer address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7364 is an Informational problem statement for NVO3. It identifies design requirements and control-plane work areas rather than defining a complete protocol.

sections.title: The Multi-Tenant Data Center Problem
sections.content:
A tenant is an administrative entity whose virtual network and services are managed in a data center. Each tenant expects its traffic and address space to remain separate from other tenants, except at controlled gateways.

Virtual machines need to move without changing their network addresses or being confined to the physical underlay subnet. The RFC presents these needs as the problem statement for Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3), which targets overlays over an IP underlay.
sections.plainLanguage: Several tenants share one data center, but each needs a separate network. A virtual machine should also be able to move without changing its network identity.

sections.title: Problems with Physical Network Designs
sections.content:
The RFC identifies problems with dynamic provisioning, virtual-machine mobility, forwarding-table size, and coupling between logical networks and physical layout. A moved virtual machine may need to keep its IP and MAC addresses, even though physical network addresses often depend on location.

Tenants also need to reuse addresses without colliding with each other or the underlay. After a move, the best gateway may change, while stateful middleboxes can constrain the route traffic must take.
sections.plainLanguage: Physical network layouts can tie addresses to locations and fill forwarding tables with individual machine entries. That makes moves and tenant address reuse difficult.

sections.title: How an Overlay Carries Tenant Traffic
sections.content:
An overlay gives each virtual network a separate address space and limits packet delivery to that network, except through controlled entry and exit points. The first-hop Network Virtualization Edge (NVE) maps a tenant destination to the underlay address of the egress NVE.

The ingress NVE encapsulates the original packet. The IP underlay forwards using the outer address, and the egress NVE removes the encapsulation and delivers the original packet. An overlay identifier tells the egress which virtual network the packet belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: The first edge finds which remote edge serves the destination and wraps the packet for the trip across the IP network. The remote edge unwraps it and delivers it inside the right virtual network.

sections.title: Design and Control-Plane Work Areas
sections.content:
The overlay should support many distributed access switches, many virtual networks with sparse membership, and tenant systems that change frequently. It should support incremental deployment, fit existing data-center operations, and not require underlay multicast.

The RFC identifies three control-plane work areas: the Network Virtualization Authority (NVA) that maintains mappings, the protocol between NVEs and the NVA, and the process for attaching or detaching tenant systems. Existing encapsulation formats can be reused rather than creating another one without a compelling reason.
sections.plainLanguage: An overlay needs a scalable way to keep track of where tenant systems are connected. It should also be possible to add it without changing the whole data center.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The problem statement does not introduce security risks by itself, but it says proposed solutions must address both data-plane and control-plane security. Data-plane concerns include tenant isolation, spoofing, snooping, packet modification, and denial of service.

Control-plane protection must prevent unauthorized parties from compromising the protocols in ways that affect packet forwarding. Some environments may also require confidentiality for control-plane information.
sections.plainLanguage: An overlay solution must keep tenants separated and protect the information that controls packet delivery. This document lists security needs but does not define their solutions.
